title: Getting Your Trademark Declared Well-Known in India: How the Rule 124 Route Actually Works
meta_description: How a brand owner applies under Rule 124 for well-known trademark status, and what the Vistara ruling means if a court already decided it.
intro: A trademark recognised as well-known gets a form of protection that an ordinary registered mark does not: the Registry is expected to refuse registration of an identical or deceptively similar mark across all classes of goods and services, not merely the classes the original mark is actually registered or used in. For a brand that has built recognition well beyond its core product category, this cross-class protection is often worth far more than a routine infringement suit against one copycat at a time.

Before 2017, the only way to get this status was to litigate it, through an opposition, rectification or infringement proceeding where a court or the Registrar happened to make a finding that the mark was well-known. The Trade Marks Rules, 2017 created a direct, non-adversarial route through Rule 124, letting a brand owner apply to the Registrar for this determination without waiting for a dispute to arise. This guide explains how that process works, what it costs, and what the Delhi High Court decided when a brand that had already won well-known status in court tried to skip the Rule 124 process altogether.

sections.heading: What Rule 124 actually lets you do
paragraphs: Rule 124 of the Trade Marks Rules, 2017 allows any person to apply to the Registrar, on Form TM-M, for a determination that a trademark is well-known. The application must be accompanied by a statement of case along with all the evidence the applicant relies on to support the claim, which typically covers the volume and duration of sales under the mark, the extent of advertising and promotional spend, the geographical area of use, evidence of registration in other jurisdictions, and any prior recognition the mark has received from courts or tribunals.

Once the Registrar is satisfied the application and evidence are in order, the Rules require the Registrar to invite objections from the general public before making a final determination, which is what distinguishes this route from an ordinary trademark application. If the mark is then declared well-known, it is published in the Trade Marks Journal and added to the Registry's list of well-known trademarks, a list that examiners are expected to check when assessing new applications for conflicting marks.

sections.heading: The cost and why it is deliberately high
paragraphs: The official fee for a Rule 124 application is one lakh rupees, a figure well above the fee for an ordinary trademark application or renewal, and it is meant to filter the process toward brand owners genuinely prepared to compile a serious evidentiary case rather than using it as a low-cost alternative to building a proper trademark portfolio. Applicants should budget for this fee alongside the cost of assembling the supporting evidence, which for a mark with a long history can itself be a significant undertaking, particularly where advertising spend and sales figures need to be certified or supported by audited records.

A well-prepared application substantially shortens the process, since the Registrar's examination and the public objection window both move faster when the statement of case is thorough from the outset. A thin application, by contrast, invites objections and requests for further evidence that can draw the process out considerably longer than a brand owner typically expects.

sections.heading: What happens if a court has already declared your mark well-known
paragraphs: This was the exact question in Tata SIA Airlines Limited v. Union of India, decided by the Delhi High Court on 25 May 2023. Tata SIA's VISTARA mark had already been declared well-known by a court in an earlier infringement suit against an unrelated party, and the company argued that once a court has made this determination under Section 11(8) of the Trade Marks Act, there is no need to separately apply through Form TM-M and pay the Rule 124 fee to get the mark onto the Registry's list.

The Registry had taken the position that a court declaration and Registry recognition are two distinct, independent routes to well-known status, each governed by its own provision, Section 11(8) for courts and Rule 124 for the Registrar, and that inclusion on the Registry's published list specifically requires going through the Rule 124 process regardless of what a court has already found. The Delhi High Court agreed with the Registry on this point and dismissed the writ petition, holding that even where a mark has been declared well-known by a court, Rule 124 continues to apply for the purpose of getting it onto the Registry's maintained list, though the Court did carve out that the specific evidence-gathering and public-objection steps under Rule 124(4) and (5) need not be repeated where a court has already made the underlying factual determination.

sections.heading: What this means practically for a brand that has already litigated well-known status
paragraphs: A brand owner who has secured a court finding of well-known status in an infringement or passing-off suit should not assume that finding automatically appears on the Registry's published list, since the Delhi High Court's ruling means a separate Form TM-M filing is still required to get there. Skipping this step leaves the brand with a court judgment that is useful in future litigation involving that specific defendant or similar facts, but without the administrative benefit of appearing on the Registry's list that examiners actually consult when screening new trademark applications across all classes.

Because the Court held that the detailed evidence-gathering and public-objection procedure need not be repeated where the underlying facts have already been judicially determined, the TM-M filing in this situation is considerably lighter than a fresh application starting from scratch, since the statement of case can largely rely on and attach the court's own judgment rather than reassembling the full evidentiary record.

sections.heading: Building the evidentiary record before you file
paragraphs: Brand owners considering a Rule 124 application from scratch should start assembling evidence well before filing, since the strength of the statement of case is what determines both the speed of the process and its ultimate success. Sales figures broken down by year and territory, advertising and marketing expenditure with supporting invoices, evidence of unsolicited media coverage or industry recognition, registration certificates from other jurisdictions where the mark is also registered, and any consumer survey evidence all strengthen the application considerably.

Evidence of enforcement history, prior successful oppositions or infringement actions taken to protect the mark, also helps, since it demonstrates the brand owner has actively policed the mark rather than passively allowed dilution, which is a factor the Registrar is entitled to weigh when assessing whether the mark has truly achieved the kind of public recognition Section 11(6) to 11(9) of the Act contemplates.

sections.heading: What happens after a mark is declared well-known
paragraphs: Once declared and published, the mark's well-known status is not permanent in an unconditional sense; it remains open to a third party to challenge the inclusion or seek removal if circumstances genuinely change, though in practice successful challenges to an already-published well-known mark are uncommon given the evidentiary threshold the brand owner had to clear to get there in the first place. Brand owners should still monitor the Trade Marks Journal periodically for any application seeking to register a conflicting mark in an unrelated class, since well-known status strengthens an opposition considerably but does not eliminate the need to actually file one when a conflicting application appears.

A brand that stops using the mark altogether, or allows its recognition to lapse substantially over a long period, could in principle face a weaker basis for relying on well-known status in a future dispute, so continued and documented use remains relevant even after the Registry's determination has been made and published.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to apply for well-known trademark status in India?
faqs.a: The official fee for a Rule 124 application on Form TM-M is one lakh rupees. This is significantly higher than ordinary trademark filing fees and is intended to limit the process to applicants with a genuine, well-documented claim.

faqs.q: If a court has already declared my mark well-known, do I still need to apply under Rule 124?
faqs.a: Yes. The Delhi High Court in the Tata SIA Airlines case held that a court declaration and Registry recognition are separate routes, and a Form TM-M filing is still needed to get the mark onto the Registry's published list, though the detailed evidence and objection steps need not be repeated.

faqs.q: What evidence does the Registry actually look at when deciding a Rule 124 application?
faqs.a: Sales volume and duration, advertising and promotional spend, geographical spread of use, registrations in other countries, unsolicited recognition or media coverage, and any prior enforcement history. A thorough statement of case supported by documentary evidence moves the process along considerably faster.

faqs.q: Does well-known status protect my mark in every class of goods and services automatically?
faqs.a: Once declared and published, the Registry is expected to refuse conflicting applications across classes, but the brand owner should still monitor the Trade Marks Journal and file oppositions where needed. Well-known status strengthens an opposition significantly but does not remove the need to actually bring one.

references: Tata SIA Airlines Limited v. Union of India, W.P.(C)-IPD 64/2021, Delhi High Court, 25 May 2023

Confirmed the Tata SIA Airlines v. Union of India decision (Delhi High Court, 25 May 2023, W.P.(C)-IPD 64/2021), its holding that Rule 124 applies even where a court has already declared a mark well-known, and the carve-out for sub-rules (4) and (5) from SSRana and World Trademark Review summaries.
